title: 2026-11-17_Sofacy_Fysbis_Backdoor_Investigation_167
description: You are an incident responder tasked with investigating a compromised Linux host that appears to be infected with the Sofacy Fysbis backdoor. Your goal is to identify and analyze the malicious activity, understand the backdoor's behavior, and take appropriate containment measures.
outcomes: Identify suspicious services and their associated files.
Contain the threat without disrupting legitimate services.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: You are an incident responder tasked with investigating a compromised Linux host that appears to be infected with the Sofacy Fysbis backdoor. Your goal is to identify and analyze the malicious activity, understand the backdoor's behavior, and take appropriate containment measures.

levels.title: Suspicious Service Discovery
levels.content: Security monitoring has detected an unusual network-facing component on the compromised host. Investigate the running services and identify the service responsible for the suspicious activity.
levels.solution:
1. List all services:
```bash
systemctl list-units --type=service --all
```
This command will display all services, including inactive ones.

2. Filter for active services:
```bash
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running
```
Look for any unfamiliar or suspicious service names.

3. Inspect the suspicious service:
```bash
systemctl cat ksysdefd.service
```
This command will show the service configuration file, which includes the ExecStart command that launches the service.

4. Identify the service name:
The service name is `ksysdefd.service`.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Use `systemctl list-units --type=service --all` to list all services, including inactive ones.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Filter the list to show only running services using `systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running`.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: Inspect the suspicious service configuration with `systemctl cat <service>`.

levels.title: C2 Communication Discovery (Port)
levels.content: An unfamiliar network service appears to be involved in unauthorized communication with an external system. Investigate the service and determine the network port associated with this communication.
levels.solution:
1. Inspect the suspicious service configuration:
```bash
systemctl cat ksysdefd.service
```
Look for the `ExecStart` line, which specifies the command launched by the service.

2. Identify the port number:
The `ExecStart` line includes the port number as an argument. In this case, it is `80`.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Use `systemctl cat <service>` to inspect the service configuration file.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Look for the `ExecStart` line in the service configuration file.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The port number is specified as an argument in the `ExecStart` command.

levels.title: Persistence Discovery for Data Collection Service
levels.content: Investigators suspect that unauthorized activity automatically resumes after the system starts and continues to execute periodically. Determine which system component is responsible for scheduling this activity.
levels.solution:
1. List all timers:
```bash
systemctl list-timers --all
```
This command will display all timers, including inactive ones.

2. Filter for active timers:
```bash
systemctl list-timers --state=active
```
Look for any unfamiliar or suspicious timer names.

3. Inspect the suspicious timer:
```bash
systemctl cat local-inventory.timer
```
This command will show the timer configuration file, which includes the schedule and the service it triggers.

4. Identify the timer name:
The timer name is `local-inventory.timer`.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Use `systemctl list-timers --all` to list all timers, including inactive ones.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Filter the list to show only active timers using `systemctl list-timers --state=active`.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: Inspect the suspicious timer configuration with `systemctl cat <timer>`.
